vars.label: Months until night-time light came back after the hurricane
vars.ref: Calculated by the observatory from NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 (collection 2) monthly night-time light, as read by nightlights.py (pixels of about 460 m, pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico); Román et al. (2018)
vars.definition: The months from the hurricane's month (September) until the area's night-time light was back to at least 80% of the same month the year before, two months in a row. 1 means back by October. The year 2017 is Hurricane María (with Irma earlier that month); 2022 is Hurricane Fiona. Each month after the storm is compared with the same month in the twelve months before the storm month (September to August). Light counts as back in the first month after September when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September (1 means back by October). Areas with a mean under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr in the year before are too dim to read and have no figure. Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power. It can stay lower after a storm because homes were left empty, businesses closed or streetlights were changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of), and a month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage shorter than a few weeks barely shows. The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).

vars.definition: The area's darkest month from September to March after the hurricane, as a share of the same month the year before. 100 means no drop; a low share means a deep blackout that lasted most of a month. Areas with a mean under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr in the year before are too dim to read and have no figure. Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power. It can stay lower after a storm because homes were left empty, businesses closed or streetlights were changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of), and a month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage shorter than a few weeks barely shows. The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).
